statistical-question.recognize.root_reason: Uses only the everyday idea of asking a question about a group and getting different answers from different individuals; no earlier node in the map supplies the idea that data vary, and the data nodes only organize and count categories.

edges.why: The statement defines a distribution as the values collected to answer a statistical question, so the learner must know what such a question is.
The test problem gives the data as a dot plot, and center, spread and shape are described from the values read off the plot.
Shape is one of the three features of a distribution, and the statement sorts shapes by how the two sides about the center look.
A symmetric distribution is defined by two sides about the center being mirror images, which is the matching-halves idea of a line of symmetry.
The test problem shows the three distributions as dot plots, so the piles of dots and the long tails must be read from the plots.
A measure of center turns the informal idea of where a distribution's values center into one number, and the test contrasts it with spread.
A measure of variation is one number for how far a distribution's values spread, the feature first described informally as spread.
Each dot sits above a position on a number line, so its value is read from where it falls on a labeled whole-number scale.
Step 2 counts the values falling in each interval, which is counting the objects in each category.
Deciding which interval a value belongs to, including a value on a boundary, means comparing the value with the interval ends.
Step 3 draws a number line marked at the interval boundaries, so values must be placed on a labeled scale.
Step 4 draws a bar up to its count on a vertical count scale over each interval, the same act as drawing a bar graph.
Each bar's height is read against the vertical count scale exactly as a category's count is read from a bar graph.
The interval that each bar covers is found from the labeled number line beneath the bars.
Step 1 draws a number line whose scale covers the minimum and maximum, and steps 2 to 4 mark values on it.
The line across the box marks the median, so the statement uses what the median of a data set is.
The box runs from the lower quartile to the upper quartile, so the statement uses what the quartiles of a data set are.
Each of the five values is read from where the end of a whisker, the box or the inside line falls on the number line.
The statement says the line inside the box is read as the median, so it uses what the median of a data set is.
The statement says the ends of the box are read as the lower and upper quartiles, so it uses what the quartiles are.
Finding the number of observations means counting the recorded values one at a time, with a repeated value counted each time it occurs.
Naming the attribute measured on each individual uses the idea that an individual has several measurable attributes, one of which was chosen.
The test problem's trip times need a unit of time, and choosing minutes over hours or seconds uses their relative sizes.
Step 1 adds all the values of the data set, which is finding a sum of several whole numbers.
Step 2 counts the number of values, with repeated values counted each time they occur.
Step 3 divides the sum by the number of values, a whole-number division whose method does not matter.
Step 1 lists the values from least to greatest, which means deciding which of two values is greater.
Steps 2 and 3 depend on the number of values, with repeated values counted each time.
The statement separates an odd number of values from an even number, and an odd count leaves one middle value when values are paired from both ends.
Step 3 takes the number halfway between the two middle values of the ordered list.
Step 1 finds the median, and step 4 finds the median of each half, so the median procedure is carried out three times.
Step 1 finds the lower quartile and the upper quartile, which are the two numbers the IQR is made from.
Step 2 subtracts the lower quartile from the upper quartile, a whole-number difference.
Steps 1 and 3 each find a mean, first of the data values and then of the distances from that mean.
Step 2 finds each value's distance from the mean as the larger number minus the smaller.
Describing where most values lie, clusters and gaps goes beyond center, spread and shape of a distribution, and a striking deviation is a value far from where the rest lie.
The explanation that every value enters the sum uses the mean as the sum of the values divided by their number.
The explanation that the median depends only on the middle position uses the median as the middle of the ordered values.
The statement compares the mean with the median as summaries, so it uses what the mean of a data set is.
The statement compares the median with the mean as summaries, so it uses what the median of a data set is.
The choice is about which number better describes a typical value, which is the job of a measure of center.
The rule is stated for roughly symmetric and strongly skewed distributions, so the learner must tell these shapes apart.
The rule depends on whether the distribution has outliers, values that depart strikingly from the overall pattern.
The reason the median better describes a typical value for skewed data is that extreme values pull the mean but barely move the median.
The statement chooses between the IQR and the MAD, so it uses what the IQR of a data set is.
The statement chooses between the IQR and the MAD, so it uses what the MAD of a data set is.
The choice is about which number better describes variability, which is the job of a measure of variation.
The rule is stated for strongly skewed and roughly symmetric distributions, so the learner must tell these shapes apart.
The rule depends on whether the distribution has outliers, values that depart strikingly from the overall pattern.
The reason extreme values inflate the MAD but not the IQR parallels how an extreme value pulls the mean but not the median.
The statement reads the MAD as a typical distance from the mean, so it uses the MAD as the mean of the distances of values from the mean.
A small MAD meaning values close to the mean and a larger MAD meaning values farther away is the meaning of a measure of variation.
The population is defined as the whole group a statistical question is about, so the learner must know what a statistical question is.
A representative sample is a sample that is like its population for the characteristic studied, so both terms must be known.
A random sample is chosen from the population so that every member has the same chance, which uses the terms population and sample.
The statement explains how choosing at random favors no part of the population, which is the equal-chance meaning of a random sample.
The statement says random sampling tends to produce representative samples, so it uses what a representative sample is.
A sample statistic and the matching population statistic are defined from the sample and from the population.
A random sample's statistic estimates the population's because random samples tend to be representative, yet any one sample can differ by chance.
The test problem gives sample means and a population mean, so the learner must know what a mean is.
The procedure uses the spread of several sample means as evidence of how far one sample mean can be from the population mean.
Step 1 draws several random samples, so the learner must know what makes a sample random.
Step 2 computes the mean of each sample.
Step 3 finds how far apart the least and greatest sample means are, which is a difference between two numbers.
The test problem's sample means are decimals in tenths, so picking the least and greatest means compares decimals.
The test problem needs the difference between decimal sample means such as 4.8 and 4.1, and any method for subtracting decimals will do.
The procedure uses the spread of several sample proportions as evidence of how far one sample proportion can be from the population proportion.
Step 1 draws several random samples, so the learner must know what makes a sample random.
Step 2 finds the fraction of a sample in the category of interest, such as 11 of 20 members, as a parts of size 1/b.
Step 3 picks the least and greatest proportions, and samples of the same size give fractions with the same denominator.
Step 3 finds how far apart the least and greatest proportions are, a difference of fractions with like denominators.
The estimate is the mean of the sample values, found as their sum divided by their number.
The statement uses a sample mean as an estimate of the population mean, the estimating relation between sample and population statistics.
Using the sample mean as an estimate is justified only because data from a random sample tend to be representative of the population.
The estimate is the fraction of the sample in a category, such as 30 of 50, written as a parts of size 1/b.
The statement uses a sample proportion as an estimate of the population proportion, the estimating relation between sample and population statistics.
Using the sample fraction as an estimate is justified only because data from a random sample tend to be representative of the population.
The statement compares two distributions by their plots, using the center, spread and shape that describe a distribution.
The statement compares the difference between two centers, so each center must be understood as one number summarizing a data set.
The statement sets the difference between centers against similar variability, so each spread must be understood as one number.
The test problem gives four dot plots on one scale, and their overlap is judged from where the dots lie.
The procedure takes the difference between two centers, so each center must be understood as one number summarizing a data set.
The procedure divides by a common measure of variability, so a measure of variation must be understood as one number for spread.
The statement turns the idea of a center difference compared with spread into a number of variability units.
Step 1 subtracts the smaller center from the larger center, a whole-number difference.
Step 2 divides the difference by the common measure of variability.
Step 3 reports the quotient as the number of measures of variability that separate the centers, a quotient read as a number of equal groups.
The decision judges the difference between the sample centers in units of the measure of variability rather than against zero.
Whether one population's values are generally greater depends on how little the two distributions overlap given their spread.
The centers of the random samples are used as estimates of the centers of the two populations.
The test problem gives MADs and asks for an explanation, which uses a MAD as a typical distance of values from the mean.
The test problem needs the difference between decimal means such as 6.5 and 4, and any method for subtracting decimals will do.
